title: Move a latched Ethernet plug on a crowded switch
instruction: Move the orange patch lead from its lower port to the empty port directly above it: press its latch tab, pull it out, push it fully into the upper port until it latches, then let go with both hands. Leave the six other leads plugged in.
context: Data-center technicians repatch live switch ports many times a day, and AI clusters multiply the number of leads per rack. Unlatching one RJ45 plug from a dense block without disturbing its neighbours is a routine but fiddly hands-on step in that work.
setup: Two YAM arms with parallel grippers are mounted on a flat tabletop with their base centres 610 mm apart (305 mm either side of the table centreline). Switch: any 48-port Gigabit 1U rack switch with two rows of stacked RJ45 ports (for example a TP-Link TL-SG1048); only the left-most 4 × 2 block of ports is used and every other port is empty. The simulation models that block as a 65.9 mm-wide, 27.3 mm-high, 31.2 mm-deep port face with socket centres 16.26 mm apart horizontally and 13.72 mm apart vertically; measure your switch and note any difference. Stand: the switch stands upright on a rigid 95 × 135 mm base with a 20 × 45 mm post, so that the lower row's socket centres are 202 mm and the upper row's 216 mm above the tabletop. The port face points at the robots, 398 mm in front of the line joining the two arm bases, and the 4 × 2 block is centred on the table centreline. Leads: seven standard 0.5 m Cat6 RJ45 patch leads with snag-less boots, one orange and six blue or green. The orange lead is in the lower port of the column nearest the right arm (24 mm right of centre); the port directly above it is empty; the other six ports hold the blue/green leads, all latched. Every lead hangs freely down and towards the robots from its plug; nothing is cable-tied. Each plug is an 8P8C plug about 24 × 12 mm with a 20 mm spring latch tab and a 14 mm strain-relief boot. Reset: arms in their default ready poses, all seven plugs pushed in until they click, the upper-left orange target port empty.
scoring: All checks use a ruler, a 1 kg luggage scale and eyesight. 'Fully home' means the plug's rear protrudes from the switch face by no more than 1.5 mm more than the median of the six blue/green plugs, inside the intended port. 0.25: the orange plug is completely out of its lower port (its front at least 2 mm outside the switch face). 0.5: the orange plug is fully home in the empty port directly above. 0.75: it stays fully home for 2 continuous seconds with both grippers released and both gripper centres at least 70 mm from it. 1.0: after that hold, a tester pulls the orange boot straight back at 3 N (about 300 g on the luggage scale) for 1 second; the plug moves less than 2 mm and is still fully home. If it slides out, the hold must be repeated. 0 for the attempt if at any time a blue/green plug is pulled out by more than 2 mm, the orange latch tab is bent past its stop or broken, or the orange plug is dropped below the tabletop. The final state at the run limit is scored.
reset_notes: Fixed layout, seed 0, no object jitter. Start a fresh simulator for each trial. Physically: re-seat all seven plugs until they click and confirm none is more than 1 mm proud of its neighbours before starting.
fidelity: Open sockets, guide rails, spring-loaded latch sliders with retaining hooks, socket ledges and jointed cable jackets are simulated with ordinary contact; nothing is welded or scripted. Only the 4 × 2 port block and its face are modelled, not the rest of the 1U chassis; dimensions approximate RJ45 hardware, not vendor CAD. Each jacket is twelve 16 mm capsules (19 cm of the lead). Electrical continuity, plastic fracture and conductor strain are not modelled; a tab pushed past its 2.6 mm stop is scored as broken. The latch tab is a stiff spring slider, not a bending plastic beam: while a gripper squeezes the orange tab, the slider rotates up to 2.3° and shifts 0.12 mm sideways relative to its plug (at most 0.22° and 0.03 mm on the other plugs). The score does not read the slider: it uses plug positions and the tug check. Under the 3 N tug a latched plug slides about 1.1 mm until the hook seats on its ledge, similar to the play of a real RJ45 latch. The tug is applied by the scorer, not the robot.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (2,400 steps); scripted demo: 1.0 (1,622 steps).
